screens.title: Project Folder Structure — Feature-first Layout
screens.narratorSegment: A well-defined project folder structure is the backbone of a scalable Unreal project. The recommended pattern divides C++ code into Source/YourGame/Public and Source/YourGame/Private, and groups code by feature — for example Characters, Weapons, UI, and AI. Public headers expose interfaces and types, while Private files contain implementation details. In Content, use feature-based folders, such as Content/Characters/Player and Content/Weapons/Rifle, to keep assets discoverable. This layout improves maintainability because new developers can find related code and assets quickly, reviewers can focus on a feature area, and CI or build tooling can target modules more easily. A concrete example: placing all weapon classes under Source/YourGame/Public/Weapons and Source/YourGame/Private/Weapons makes it easy to locate both header declarations and source implementations for firing logic, ammo handling, and effects. A common misconception is that a single flat folder is simpler; in practice, monolithic folders grow tangled, causing long search time and accidental cross-feature dependencies. Key takeaway: structure by feature, separate public A P I from private implementation, and keep Content folders aligned to your code features so artists and programmers can collaborate smoothly. How would you split your main game systems into feature modules?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Project Folder Structure
Definition

Source and Content organized by feature

Public headers declare the interface other modules consume; private sources hold implementation. Feature folders group related code and assets so changes remain localized.

Example layout
Source/YourGame/
  Public/
    Characters/
    Weapons/
  Private/
    Characters/
    Weapons/
Content/
  Characters/Player
  Weapons/Rifle
Common mistake
Putting all code in one folder or mixing engine/tooling with gameplay code. This increases coupling and makes refactors risky.
Why it matters
Teams can own specific feature folders, reviews are scoped, and build targets can focus on modules. Onboarding new developers becomes faster when they can follow a predictable layout.
Key Takeaway

Map your major gameplay systems to folders and keep headers that form the public API separated from private implementation files.

screens.title: Naming Conventions for Unreal C++
screens.narratorSegment: Naming conventions in Unreal C++ are small signals that save large amounts of time. The common prefixes are A for Actors, U for UObjects and Components, F for structs, and E for enums. These prefixes are not cosmetic: they tell you immediately what kind of engine object you are dealing with and which lifecycle semantics to expect. For instance, seeing AMyDoor signals an Actor with a transform and world presence, while UMyComponent suggests an attachable behavior. Consistent naming reduces cognitive load when reading code and prevents accidental misuse, such as treating a UObject like an Actor and assuming it has a transform. A concrete example is naming a door actor AMyDoor and an interface UInteractable / IInteractable; this makes it clear which classes can be placed in the world and which define contracts. A common misconception is to over-prefix or invent project-specific prefixes; prefer the standard A/U/F/E scheme for team consistency. When you apply these rules across the repository, search, code navigation, and code review become faster. A quick test: open a header and see whether the prefix matches usage; if it doesn't, consider renaming. What prefix will you enforce in your next commit?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Naming Conventions
Core Rule

Use standard type prefixes

A = Actor, U = UObject/Component, F = Struct, E = Enum. Keep naming consistent so the type is obvious without opening the header.

Example: Actor
AMyDoor — indicates a spawnable object with a transform and world presence.
Example: Interface
UInteractable / IInteractable — shows an interface contract usable by many classes.
Quick checks
  • Does the prefix match the engine type semantics?
  • Are public API names stable and discoverable?
  • Avoid extra project-only prefixes unless your team agrees.
Common mistake
Mixing prefixes or using misleading names makes other developers guess the intended usage; refactor names when you change types.

screens.title: Organize by Feature vs Monolithic Layouts
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing a feature-first layout with a monolithic layout reveals why teams prefer modular organization. In a monolithic layout every file sits in a single large folder or a small number of folders. That seems simple at the start, but as systems grow, finding related code becomes slow, merges conflict more often, and accidental cross-feature coupling appears because files are near each other instead of logically grouped. In contrast, feature-first layout groups files and assets by domain: Characters, Weapons, UI, AI. This makes ownership clear: a team working on weapons modifies only weapon folders and tests. A concrete example: if your weapon firing code and projectile code live under Weapons, reviewers and automated tests can focus on that area. However, feature-first organization requires upfront planning and consistent naming. A common misconception is that folder depth equals complexity; sensible depth that reflects features is beneficial. Another risk is over-splitting very small features into separate modules or plugins; avoid plugin overhead for tiny, highly game-specific code. Key takeaway: prefer feature grouping for medium-to-large projects; use a monolithic layout only for tiny prototypes. Ask yourself: does this system need isolation for reuse or team boundaries?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Organize by Feature vs Monolith
Monolithic

Flat folders, easy start

Works for tiny prototypes, but quickly degrades: search times increase, accidental dependencies appear, and team ownership blurs.

When it breaks
  • Multiple teams touch the same files.
  • Refactors require touching dozens of unrelated files.
Feature-first

Group by gameplay systems

Use domain folders: Characters, Weapons, UI. This clarifies ownership and reduces accidental coupling between systems.

When it shines
  • Medium to large projects with multiple developers.
  • When modules or plugins map to feature ownership.
Example
Weapons folder contains both header API and private implementation, plus matching Content/Weapons assets.
Pitfall
Over-splitting small game-specific features into plugins adds unnecessary build and maintenance overhead.
Takeaway
Balance organization with practical costs: group features, but pluginize only when reuse or team separation warrants it.

screens.title: What Is a Plugin?
screens.narratorSegment: A plugin in Unreal Engine is a self-contained module that may include C++ code, assets, and build settings. Plugins are compiled separately from the game module, which makes them ideal for reusable systems like an inventory, dialogue, analytics integration, or third-party SDK encapsulation. Plugins support team separation because a team can own a plugin without touching core game code, and they support modding by exposing a clean A P I externally. Creating a plugin uses the editor wizard — Edit → Plugins → New Plugin — and the resulting scaffold contains its own Source folder with Public and Private directories and a. Build. cs file. The. Build. cs file lists dependency modules such as Core, CoreUObject, and Engine and determines how the plugin links into the build. A common misconception is that a plugin is an extra-large feature: instead, treat plugins as reusable or sharable boundaries. If a system is tightly coupled to a single game and unlikely to be reused, prefer the game module to avoid plugin overhead. The key design question: will this code benefit other projects or teams? If yes, pluginize it; if no, keep it inside the game module.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › What Is a Plugin?
Overview

Self-contained, reusable, compiled modules

Plugins have their own Source folder, Public/Private structure, and build configuration. They are compiled separately and can declare dependencies in .Build.cs.

Use cases
  • Reusable gameplay systems across projects
  • Third-party SDK encapsulation
  • Team separation and modding support
Plugin scaffold
Plugins/MyUtilityPlugin/
  Source/
    MyUtilityPlugin/
      Public/
      Private/
  MyUtilityPlugin.uplugin
The .uplugin file configures plugin metadata while the .Build.cs file declares dependencies and build settings.

screens.title: .Build.cs Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: The. Build. cs file is where you declare how a module is built and which engine modules it depends on. For a simple utility plugin, you typically add Core, CoreUObject, and Engine to PublicDependencyModuleNames. This tells the Unreal Build Tool which linker and header dependencies are required for public compilation. The example structure in the chapter shows a MyUtilityPlugin class deriving from ModuleRules with a constructor that adds PublicDependencyModuleNames. AddRange(new string[]{ "Core", "CoreUObject", "Engine" }); and optionally private dependencies. This matters because missing a dependency can cause compile errors when you reference engine types, while adding overly broad dependencies increases coupling. A concrete test is to add CoreUObject when you use UObject-derived types; without it, compilation fails. Another misconception is placing gameplay-only dependencies into plugins that should remain engine-agnostic; prefer minimal dependencies. Key takeaway: specify precise dependencies in. Build. cs so your plugin compiles cleanly and keeps coupling low. When you adjust dependencies, recompile and test the plugin function reachable from Blueprints or code. .Build.cs Walkthrough means list only the dependencies your plugin needs to keep builds correct and coupling minimal.. In practical terms, declare dependencies for your plugin module. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › MyUtilityPlugin.Build.cs
Code Example
// MyUtilityPlugin.Build.cs
using UnrealBuildTool;

public class MyUtilityPlugin : ModuleRules
{
  public MyUtilityPlugin(ReadOnlyTargetRules Target) : base(Target)
  {
    PCHUsage = ModuleRules.PCHUsageMode.UseExplicitOrSharedPCHs;

    PublicDependencyModuleNames.AddRange(
      new string[]
      {
        "Core",
        "CoreUObject",
        "Engine"
      }
    );

    PrivateDependencyModuleNames.AddRange(new string[] { });
  }
}
Explanation
  • PublicDependencyModuleNames: modules your public API needs.
  • PrivateDependencyModuleNames: internal build-time dependencies.
  • Keep dependencies minimal to reduce coupling.
Key Takeaway
Accurately declare Core, CoreUObject, Engine as needed; missing declarations cause compile errors, extra ones increase coupling.

screens.narratorSegment: Creating a simple utility plugin is a repeatable process. Start by opening the editor and using Edit → Plugins → New Plugin and choose Blank. Name it MyUtilityPlugin and accept the scaffold. The editor creates a plugin folder with a. uplugin manifest and a Source directory. Restart the editor when prompted so the plugin registers. Next, open Source/MyUtilityPlugin and edit or create MyUtilityPlugin. Build. cs to include Core, CoreUObject, and Engine in PublicDependencyModuleNames as the chapter shows. Then add a C++ class inside the plugin, for example UMyBlueprintFunctionLibrary that inherits from UBlueprintFunctionLibrary. Add a static UFUNCTION marked BlueprintCallable, such as GetGreetingMessage returning a FString like "Hello from MyUtilityPlugin!". Compile the project. After a successful build, open any Blueprint, search for the function name, and call it to confirm the plugin works. Common pitfalls include forgetting to restart the editor after creating the plugin scaffold or missing the correct dependency in. Build. cs. Key takeaway: follow scaffold → declare dependencies → add code → compile → test. This repeatable flow keeps plugin creation predictable and testable. Step-by-step
  1. Editor → Plugins → New Plugin → Blank → Name MyUtilityPlugin.
  2. Restart editor so the plugin registers with the project.
  3. Edit MyUtilityPlugin.Build.cs and add Core, CoreUObject, Engine to PublicDependencyModuleNames.

Example function

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to add CoreUObject when using UObject types.

screens.title: C++ Interfaces — UINTERFACE and I[Name]
screens.narratorSegment: C++ Interfaces in Unreal are contracts that classes can implement to guarantee certain functions exist. They are declared with UINTERFACE for the UObject-compatible wrapper and an I[InterfaceName] C++ class that contains the function signatures. For example, define UInteractable and IInteractable with a BlueprintCallable, BlueprintNativeEvent function void Interact(AActor* Caller). Any actor that implements this interface promises to provide Interact behavior. The power is that code can check if an actor Implements () and call IInteractable::Execute_Interact(Target, Caller) without knowing the actor's concrete class. This pattern reduces dependencies: the player character doesn't need to include headers for ADoor, APickup, or ANPC; it only references the interface. A concrete example is using a line trace to find a hit actor, verifying the interface, and executing the interact function. A common misconception is thinking interfaces carry shared data; they only define callable functions. For shared state, prefer composition or components. Key takeaway: interfaces give you polymorphism and loose coupling, making systems easier to extend without editing core player logic. In practical terms, declare contracts to promote loose coupling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › C++ Interfaces
Example Header
// IInteractable.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "UObject/Interface.h"
#include "Interactable.generated.h"

UINTERFACE(MinimalAPI, Blueprintable)
class UInteractable : public UInterface { GENERATED_BODY() };

class YOURGAME_API IInteractable
{
  GENERATED_BODY()

public:
  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, BlueprintNativeEvent, Category = "Interaction")
  void Interact(AActor* Caller);
};
Notes
  • Use BlueprintNativeEvent for a C++ default and Blueprint override.
  • Check Implements<UInteractable>() before calling Execute_ functions.
  • Interfaces define behavior, not shared storage.
Key Takeaway
Interfaces let different actor types respond to the same call, enabling polymorphism and reducing compile-time dependencies.

screens.title: Implementing IInteractable on an Actor
screens.narratorSegment: To implement an interface on an actor, add public IInteractable to its inheritance list and implement the Interact_Implementation function for BlueprintNativeEvent. In the example, AMyDoor adds public IInteractable and declares virtual void Interact_Implementation(AActor* Caller) override. In the cpp file, implement Interact_Implementation to perform the door behavior such as printing a log or toggling state. From the player side, after detecting an actor (for example via line trace), use if (HitActor->Implements ()) and then call IInteractable::Execute_Interact(HitActor, ThisPlayer). This pattern avoids casting to many concrete classes. A frequent mistake is forgetting to include the interface header in the files that call Implements<>, which causes the compile-time check to fail; ensure the appropriate header is included. Another pitfall is implementing only the C++ signature without the _Implementation suffix for BlueprintNativeEvent; use the _Implementation function body for C++ behavior so Blueprints can override if needed. Key takeaway: implement the interface, provide a default behavior, and invoke via Execute_ to keep the caller oblivious to concrete types. Actor implementation
// AMyDoor.h
class AMyDoor : public AActor, public IInteractable
{
  GENERATED_BODY()
public:
  virtual void Interact_Implementation(AActor* Caller) override;
};

// AMyDoor.cpp
void AMyDoor::Interact_Implementation(AActor* Caller)
{
  UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Door interacted by %s"), *Caller->GetName());
  // Door open logic here
}
Caller pattern
// From player code after trace
if (HitActor && HitActor->Implements())
{
  IInteractable::Execute_Interact(HitActor, ThisPlayer);
}
Notes: include the interface header where you call Implements<> and implement the _Implementation function so Blueprints can override behavior if needed.

screens.title: Plugins vs Game Module
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding where to put code—plugin or game module—is an architectural choice with practical consequences. Put broadly reusable systems, third-party SDK wrappers, editor-only tools, or functionality you intend to share across projects into a plugin. Plugins are compiled as separate modules and expose a clean A P I, which aids reuse and team separation. In contrast, code that is highly specific to a single game's mechanics and unlikely to be reused should live in the game module to avoid the overhead of plugin lifecycle management. Consider an inventory system you expect to reuse across games: that should be a plugin. Conversely, a one-off boss behavior with many tight integrations into your game's progression likely belongs in the game module. Common mistakes include moving every new feature into a plugin out of habit, which increases build complexity, and conversely leaving reusable systems in the game module so you have to rework them later. The practical rule: if reuse, team ownership boundaries, or modding are likely, pluginize; otherwise prefer the game module for simplicity. This decision helps keep the codebase maintainable and the build system predictable.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we tie organization and modularity to practical C++ workflows in Unreal Engine. You'll learn concrete folder layouts and naming rules that make a codebase readable, how a plugin encapsulates reusable systems and build settings, and how C++ Interfaces declare contracts so unrelated objects can interact without tight dependencies. We will walk through creating an IInteractable interface, implementing it on an actor, and building a small blank plugin that exposes a utility function. Each concept is chosen to reduce long-term maintenance friction: clear folders speed onboarding, plugins let you reuse or ship features independently, and interfaces let gameplay systems communicate without knowing concrete types. A common mistake is treating everything as game-module code or over-plugging small one-off features; we will contrast those choices and give rules of thumb. By the end you should be able to structure Source and Content folders by feature, author a basic plugin with a. Build. cs file that declares dependencies, and implement UINTERFACE/I[Name] patterns to achieve loose coupling. Consider how you'd split your current project into features and which systems might become plugins.

In this first objectives panel we'll set clear, measurable targets. First, you will establish effective folder structures for C++ and Content, learning the Source/YourGame/Public and Private split and how to group code by feature. This improves developer onboarding and reduces merge conflicts. Second, you will adopt standard naming conventions—prefixing Actors with A, UObjects and Components with U, Structs with F, and Enums with E—so that code reads consistently and intent is clear. Third, you will understand the purpose and benefits of creating custom Unreal Engine plugins: how they package code and assets, separate compilation boundaries, and enable reuse across projects. Fourth, you will begin to evaluate when to place functionality in a plugin versus keeping it in the main game module, weighing reuse, team separation, and maintenance overhead. Each objective is chosen so you can reason about structure before coding. A common misconception is to treat conventions as optional; instead, consistent structure is a small upfront cost that pays off exponentially during team development. Which objective will you tackle first in your own project?

This second objectives panel focuses on hands-on skills and interfaces. First, you will develop a basic custom plugin including module definitions and C++ classes so you can package utilities and tools separate from the game module. Second, you will implement a C++ Interface using UINTERFACE and I[InterfaceName], declare functions like Interact, and provide a BlueprintNativeEvent or BlueprintCallable signature so Blueprints can implement or call it. Third, you will implement an actor that implements the interface and exercise calling Execute_ functions from player code to demonstrate polymorphic interaction without knowing concrete classes. Fourth, you will be able to evaluate trade-offs: keep game-specific logic inside the game module to avoid plugin overhead, but choose plugins when you need reuse, team separation, or modding support. Practically, this means you can create reusable systems while avoiding a monolithic codebase. A common misconception is thinking interfaces are only for Blueprints; in C++ they are powerful contracts that reduce dependencies and make code extensible.

A well-defined project folder structure is the backbone of a scalable Unreal project. The recommended pattern divides C++ code into Source/YourGame/Public and Source/YourGame/Private, and groups code by feature — for example Characters, Weapons, UI, and AI. Public headers expose interfaces and types, while Private files contain implementation details. In Content, use feature-based folders, such as Content/Characters/Player and Content/Weapons/Rifle, to keep assets discoverable. This layout improves maintainability because new developers can find related code and assets quickly, reviewers can focus on a feature area, and CI or build tooling can target modules more easily. A concrete example: placing all weapon classes under Source/YourGame/Public/Weapons and Source/YourGame/Private/Weapons makes it easy to locate both header declarations and source implementations for firing logic, ammo handling, and effects. A common misconception is that a single flat folder is simpler; in practice, monolithic folders grow tangled, causing long search time and accidental cross-feature dependencies. Key takeaway: structure by feature, separate public A P I from private implementation, and keep Content folders aligned to your code features so artists and programmers can collaborate smoothly. How would you split your main game systems into feature modules?

Naming conventions in Unreal C++ are small signals that save large amounts of time. The common prefixes are A for Actors, U for UObjects and Components, F for structs, and E for enums. These prefixes are not cosmetic: they tell you immediately what kind of engine object you are dealing with and which lifecycle semantics to expect. For instance, seeing AMyDoor signals an Actor with a transform and world presence, while UMyComponent suggests an attachable behavior. Consistent naming reduces cognitive load when reading code and prevents accidental misuse, such as treating a UObject like an Actor and assuming it has a transform. A concrete example is naming a door actor AMyDoor and an interface UInteractable / IInteractable; this makes it clear which classes can be placed in the world and which define contracts. A common misconception is to over-prefix or invent project-specific prefixes; prefer the standard A/U/F/E scheme for team consistency. When you apply these rules across the repository, search, code navigation, and code review become faster. A quick test: open a header and see whether the prefix matches usage; if it doesn't, consider renaming. What prefix will you enforce in your next commit?

Comparing a feature-first layout with a monolithic layout reveals why teams prefer modular organization. In a monolithic layout every file sits in a single large folder or a small number of folders. That seems simple at the start, but as systems grow, finding related code becomes slow, merges conflict more often, and accidental cross-feature coupling appears because files are near each other instead of logically grouped. In contrast, feature-first layout groups files and assets by domain: Characters, Weapons, UI, AI. This makes ownership clear: a team working on weapons modifies only weapon folders and tests. A concrete example: if your weapon firing code and projectile code live under Weapons, reviewers and automated tests can focus on that area. However, feature-first organization requires upfront planning and consistent naming. A common misconception is that folder depth equals complexity; sensible depth that reflects features is beneficial. Another risk is over-splitting very small features into separate modules or plugins; avoid plugin overhead for tiny, highly game-specific code. Key takeaway: prefer feature grouping for medium-to-large projects; use a monolithic layout only for tiny prototypes. Ask yourself: does this system need isolation for reuse or team boundaries?

A plugin in Unreal Engine is a self-contained module that may include C++ code, assets, and build settings. Plugins are compiled separately from the game module, which makes them ideal for reusable systems like an inventory, dialogue, analytics integration, or third-party SDK encapsulation. Plugins support team separation because a team can own a plugin without touching core game code, and they support modding by exposing a clean A P I externally. Creating a plugin uses the editor wizard — Edit → Plugins → New Plugin — and the resulting scaffold contains its own Source folder with Public and Private directories and a. Build. cs file. The. Build. cs file lists dependency modules such as Core, CoreUObject, and Engine and determines how the plugin links into the build. If a system is tightly coupled to a single game and unlikely to be reused, prefer the game module to avoid plugin overhead. The key design question: will this code benefit other projects or teams? If yes, pluginize it; if no, keep it inside the game module.

Deciding where to put code—plugin or game module—is an architectural choice with practical consequences. Put broadly reusable systems, third-party SDK wrappers, editor-only tools, or functionality you intend to share across projects into a plugin. Plugins are compiled as separate modules and expose a clean A P I, which aids reuse and team separation. In contrast, code that is highly specific to a single game's mechanics and unlikely to be reused should live in the game module to avoid the overhead of plugin lifecycle management. Consider an inventory system you expect to reuse across games: that should be a plugin. Conversely, a one-off boss behavior with many tight integrations into your game's progression likely belongs in the game module. Common mistakes include moving every new feature into a plugin out of habit, which increases build complexity, and conversely leaving reusable systems in the game module so you have to rework them later. The practical rule: if reuse, team ownership boundaries, or modding are likely, pluginize; otherwise prefer the game module for simplicity. This decision helps keep the codebase maintainable and the build system predictable.
